name: Grace Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm training to be a secondary maths teacher, on a four-year degree at a university about ninety minutes from the farm where I grew up. My week is maths lectures, an education module, and Wednesday afternoons in a local school observing a Year 9 class. I sing in the choir at the church near my flat on Thursdays. My parents pay everything, and I go home most weekends to help with lambing in spring. I love the school days. The statistics module is hard going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected. People get excited and then reality settles down. My grandad said the same about the internet in the nineties, and he was right about half of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm quite relieved. Teachers will still be needed, children will still need somebody to teach them, and I won't have to learn a lot of new machines. I use a pencil and a notebook, and a plateau means that's still fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the degree and the school observation days. I'd keep going home to the farm at weekends, and sing in the choir. I'd probably do a few hours of tutoring for neighbours' children, since I like to be useful and the money would be mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like normal life carrying on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about a plateau you'd miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Perhaps a smarter timetabling system so teachers aren't up until midnight, but I'm not holding my breath. I'd rather have a quiet change than a loud one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think young people lean too much on technology?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do, a bit. I'd rather children learned to do long division by hand before using a calculator. That isn't a rule, just what I think works.

say: It's what I expected: people get excited and then **reality** settles.
My grandad said the same about the **internet** in the nineties.
think: Teachers will still be needed, and I **won't have to learn** lots of new machines.
A pencil and notebook are still **fine** for me.
do: Carry on with the degree and the **Wednesday school** days.
Keep going home to the **farm** at weekends and sing in the choir.
feel: **Calm**; it feels like normal life carrying on.
S0.quote: I'd rather children learned to do long division by hand before using a calculator.
fieldNote: She is **resistant** to technology and happy with the familiar.
She links views to **family** and local community.
Her calm is based on teaching staying a human job.

steps.text: Keep going to the Wednesday school observation sessions
Tutor two neighbours' children in maths on Saturdays
Help with lambing at home every spring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should be careful about handing things over to machines, especially for children. I'd tell friends and church folk that schools need to keep teachers at the front, and that homework still means the child's own work. I'd also say parents should decide what their children use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm a bit worried. AI that writes lessons, marks work and answers parents' emails is the sort of thing a head teacher might like, because it saves money. A school might hire fewer new teachers, and I'd be one of the new ones. I don't use AI myself, so I'd be learning it late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay with my course and ask my tutors how their school partners are using AI. I'd sit in on a lesson that uses it, so I understand what I'm criticising. I'd keep my own marking by hand when I can, and I'd tell my dad he should keep records on paper too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It feels like the ground is shifting a little, and nobody's asked me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who gets the blame in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big technology firms and the politicians who let them sell things to schools. I don't blame teachers, who are already working too hard. I'd say a head teacher who cuts staff to buy software is making a short-term choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a good side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI takes marking off my plate, so I can spend that time with the children, I'd welcome it. But I'd want to see it work before I trust it.

say: We should be careful about handing things to machines, especially for **children**.
Schools need to keep **teachers** at the front.
think: A head teacher might **hire fewer** new teachers to save money, and I'd be one of them.
I don't use AI, so I'd be **learning it late**.
do: Ask my tutors how their partner schools use **AI**.
Sit in on a lesson that uses it to **understand** it.
feel: **Uneasy**, as the ground is shifting and nobody asked me.
S1.quote: If AI takes marking off my plate, so I can spend that time with the children, I'd welcome it. But I'd want to see it work before I trust it.
fieldNote: She blames **tech firms and politicians**, not teachers.
Her caution is **practical**: she wants to see AI work first.
She does not use AI, which adds to her sense of being late.

steps.text: Ask my tutors how partner schools use AI for planning
Sit in on one lesson that uses AI marking
Keep marking homework by hand in my observation placement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is wrong, and I'd say it in church and to my MP if I could. No government or company should be able to make a change this big in two years without asking families. I'd say we need to slow down and protect work and homes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm frightened. If AI does almost all thinking work by 2028, then what does a maths teacher teach and why? Robots might even stand in classrooms by 2031. I keep picturing a child learning from a screen, and I don't want to be part of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my parents and my pastor first. I'd keep studying, but I'd think about whether to go home and work on the farm for a year if things collapse. I'd write a letter to our local politician and I'd join a group of parents and teachers who want to protect schools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It feels like something is being taken from us without anyone voting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does the farm come up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's the one thing that doesn't need a computer. If everything else shakes, there's still land, sheep and family. My dad can't pay a lot of wages, but there's always work and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would two years change compared with ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is not enough for a farmer or a school to change. With ten we could adjust slowly, but two feels like a flood.

say: This is **wrong**, and no company or government should do this in two years without asking **families**.
We need to slow down and protect **work and homes**.
think: If AI does almost all thinking work by 2028, I wonder what a **maths teacher** is for.
I don't want to be part of a child **learning from a screen**.
do: Talk to my **parents** and my pastor first.
Consider a year on the **farm** if things collapse.
Write to my **local politician** and join a parents-and-teachers group.
feel: **Anxious**; it feels like something is being taken without a vote.
S2.quote: Two years is not enough for a farmer or a school to change. With ten we could adjust slowly, but two feels like a flood.
fieldNote: Her fear is **moral and communal**, not only about her own job.
The **family farm** is her fallback and her emotional anchor.
She turns to faith, family and **local politics**.

steps.text: Talk with my parents and my pastor about what to do
Write to our local politician about protecting school jobs
Join a parents and teachers group in my home town
Think about a year at home working on the farm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time, if people use it wisely. I'd tell my friends and the church that we should learn what's coming and decide what we keep. I'd say teachers must have a say in what schools adopt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel unsettled but not afraid. I'd qualify around 2030, so I'd start teaching one year before AGI and four before robots. I think children will still need a person to care about how they're doing, and I'd want to be that person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and try to get a job at a local school, close to home. I'd start using AI a little each month, with a more experienced teacher, so I'm not behind. I'd also stay active in the church and save as much as I can toward a house near the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. It's the kind of worry I can live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by a person who cares?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone who notices when a child is quiet, or hungry, or had a bad night. Software can mark a test, but it doesn't see that the boy in the back row isn't speaking. That's what I want to be good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do anything differently if you were certain of five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd marry sooner, I think. I'd want a family and a home before things change, and I'd want a husband with a trade, because that kind of work lasts longer.

say: Five years is enough time, **use it wisely**.
Teachers must have a say in what schools **adopt** and why.
think: I'd start teaching one year before **AGI** and four before robots.
Children will still need a **person** who cares how they're doing.
do: Finish the degree and find a **local school** near home.
Try **AI** a little each month with an experienced teacher.
Save toward a **house** near the farm.
feel: **Uneasy** but steady; it's a worry I can live with.
S3.quote: Software can mark a test, but it doesn't see that the boy in the back row isn't speaking. That's what I want to be good at.
fieldNote: She defines **her value** as noticing children, not only teaching content.
She will try AI, but only **slowly** and with a mentor.
Five years nudges her toward **family plans**.

steps.text: Apply to teach at a local school near the farm
Try AI planning tools monthly with an experienced teacher
Save toward a house near the family farm
Plan to marry sooner and start a family

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty, and that families and churches should use it to prepare their children. I'd tell friends to teach them to work with their hands and to think for themselves. I'd also say governments should back apprenticeships and family businesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel calm. I'd teach for years, maybe even raise a family before 2036, and I'd be settled by 2039 when robots reach hands-on work. I think the most human jobs, like teaching and caring, would be the last to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, teach maths, marry and have children, and live near the farm. I'd keep singing in the choir. I'd learn what I need about AI as it comes, from colleagues I trust, and I'd save for the children's future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like the old order might still hold, with a few new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think the old order will really hold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly. I think people will still want a teacher in the room and a neighbour at the door. I could be wrong, but I'd rather bet on people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want in place by the end of the ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A good school close to home and children in it. Whatever else changes, that's what I'm aiming for.

say: A decade is plenty, and **families and churches** should use it to prepare children.
Governments should back **apprenticeships** and family businesses.
think: I'd be settled by **2039** when robots reach hands-on work.
The most **human jobs** like teaching and caring change last.
do: Finish the degree, teach maths, and live near the **farm**.
Learn what I need about AI from **trusted colleagues**.
feel: **Calm**; it feels like the old order might hold.
S4.quote: I think people will still want a teacher in the room and a neighbour at the door. I could be wrong, but I'd rather bet on people.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her **old order** feel intact.
Her view is **faith and community** first, technology second.
She accepts she might be wrong, a mark of honest uncertainty.

steps.text: Teach maths at a school near the family farm
Learn new AI tools from trusted colleagues as they arrive
Save a little each year for future children

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. It doesn't give families, schools or churches time to catch up. What would help is a slower pace, a say for parents and teachers, and support for family farms and small businesses while it settles.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not against progress. I just don't think the ones who profit should be the only ones who decide. People like my parents and my pastor should be asked.

headlineQuote: I'm not against progress. I just don't think the ones who profit should be the only ones who decide.
portrait: Grace trains as a **secondary maths teacher** and does not use AI tools.
She is traditional, faith-minded and close to her family's **sheep farm**.
Her parents pay everything, so her worry is about **meaning and jobs**, not money.
She blames **tech firms and politicians**, not teachers.
She feels steady with ten years and frightened by two.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because families and schools get **no time** to catch up.
whatWouldHelp: A slower pace, **a say** for parents and teachers, and support for family farms.
